Measured on the same glyphs: '#', '##', and both '**' pairs around 'bottle' are one flat 50%-grey in A, loud enough to read as content next to the #CCCCCC comma beside them.
gapTheirs: B's markers land at 2.90:1 against paper — under the 3:1 floor for non-text marks — so the thinnest ones (the '*' pairs around the italic run, the '-' list bullets) go soft on a dimmed or glossy panel; A's 4.41:1 never disappears. B also has no brighter tier: one grey (#636363) serves #, ##, **, * and - alike, so a heading's scaffold and an emphasis mark carry identical weight.
verdict: Paper and ink are byte-identical here — #1A1A1A ground, #CCCCCC ink, 10.84:1 in both — so this comes down to the one grey between them, and A gets it wrong. At #808080 A's hashes and asterisks are 60% of the ink's perceptual weight; you look at '**bottle**' and read four stars before you read the word, which is the exact failure mode markdown-in-place is supposed to prevent. B's #636363 recedes into scaffolding without vanishing, which is the whole job. Neither has actually designed a dark mode though: every grey is R=G=B, the paper has no cast, the ink is left at a halating #CCCCCC, and headings share the body's colour — this is an inversion with one variable tuned, and B tuned it better.

states.gapTheirs: Marker grey #9E9E9E is 2.54:1 against #F9F9F9 paper — below the 3:1 floor for any non-text element. Every structural signal in the file (`#`, `##`, `*`, `**`) drops to a smear: you cannot count `##` against `###` at a glance, and the bookends around bold vanish so `**bottle**` reads as ink that got heavier for no stated reason.
states.verdict: These are the same page twice: 2 levels of paper apart, 3 levels of ink apart, the same 3px full-height caret. The one thing that separates them is the grey in between, and B chose a grey that quits — markers at 2.54:1 are not restraint, they are a token nudged toward the paper until it stopped doing its job, and in a plain-text editor the markers are the only structure you get. A's ramp is actually stepped — 4.0:1 paper-to-grey, 4.1:1 grey-to-ink, evenly spaced by contrast rather than by eyeballing — so the syntax recedes without disappearing. Neither of you showed me a dark mode, which is half the brief, so this is a win on the only ground either of you put on screen.
